newsitem.title: UK: UK proposes tougher anti-strike legislation.
newsitem.headline: UK proposes tougher anti-strike legislation.

text.p: The British government on Tuesday proposed new curbs on strikes following a summer of disruptions to the postal service and London Underground.

The proposals, trailed by Trade Secretary Ian Lang at last month's Conservative party conference, include removing trade unions' immunity to legal action if they organise strikes that have "disproportionate or excessive effects".

Lang, writing in the introduction to a consultative "green" paper, said that by comparison with many other countries Britain had little statutory protection against disruption of essential services by industrial action.
"The government believes there is now widespread recognition that trade unions' ability to cause unreasonable disruption to the public should be constrained."
"In deciding on industrial action, trade unions and their members pursuing a particular dispute must take account of the broader interests of the community," Lang said.
Other proposals in the green paper include:
-- raising the threshold in strike ballots from the majority of those voting to the majority of those entitled to vote.
-- requiring unions to ballot members every three months or sooner on whether long-running industrial action should continue.
-- doubling to 14 days the notice a union must give in order to be immune from the normal civil law. This would allow the public to plan better ahead of a strike, minimising disruption.
Lang said the number of days lost to strikes had fallen by 90 percent since former prime minister Margaret Thatcher started to reform Britain's industrial relations laws in 1979.

But the figure rose to 1.24 million days in the 12 months to September, higher than in the previous five years, with around 70 percent of the total in the public sector and other monopoly services where the public had no choice of supplier, Lang said.
"The right to strike has to be reconciled with the need to protect the public from being severely disrupted," Lang said. He invited comments on the proposals by February 28.
But the opposition Labour party's employment spokesman David Blunkett said they had nothing to do with settling disputes and everything to do with the run-up to the general election.

"The only people who are going to gain out of this are not businesses, are not individuals who cannot possibly sue people involved in a dispute, but the lawyers who will take their money," Blunkett told BBC radio. He said Labour favoured greater emphasis on conciliation to head off strikes.
The critical issue of what would constitute a "disproportionate or excessive" effect would be left to the courts to decide.
But the government, which will set out clear guidance in statute, said in its green paper it might be defined as involving one or a combination of:
-- risks to life, health or safety
-- threats to national security
-- serious damage to property or to the economy
-- significant disruption of everyday life or activities in the whole or part of the country.

This meant strikes would not be outlawed if a union ensured that an adequate level of service was maintained -- for example emergency cover in the health service or a safe and reasonable train service.
But the green paper also says that occasionally even actions short of an all-out strike might have disproportionate or excessive effects and would thus be illegal under its proposals.
A union that disobeyed a court injunction against a strike could be fined and have its assets sequestered.
It said a similar legal concept of proportionality exists in industrial relations law in Germany and the Netherlands.
